Block 0 · Install & Shared Dataset¶

Run once. Creates the shared literature dataset used in all later blocks.

Block 1 · Literature Data Quality Audit¶

Before doing anything else, audit your data:

  • How many records do you have per property?
  • Which properties have the most missing values?
  • Are units consistent?
  • What is the class distribution?

A data audit tells you where to focus cleaning effort.

In [3]:
# ── 1a: Missing value audit ────────────────────────────────────

numeric_cols = ['MW','Density','ImpactSens_J','DecompTemp_C',
                'DetVel_ms','HeatForm_kJmol']

df = df_raw.copy()
for col in numeric_cols:
    df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce')

# Missing value summary

    'Total':   df[numeric_cols].shape[0],
    'Missing': df[numeric_cols].isna().sum(),
    'Present': df[numeric_cols].notna().sum(),
    'Missing%': (df[numeric_cols].isna().mean() * 100).round(1),
}).reset_index().rename(columns={'index': 'Property'})

# ── 1c: Class distribution and completeness per class ──────────

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))

# Pie chart — class distribution
class_counts = df['Class'].value_counts()
colors = ['#e74c3c','#3498db','#2ecc71','#f39c12']
axes[0].pie(class_counts, labels=class_counts.index, autopct='%1.0f%%',
            colors=colors, startangle=90)
axes[0].set_title('Class Distribution (n=30)')

# Stacked bar — data completeness per class
comp = df.groupby('Class')[numeric_cols].apply(lambda g: g.notna().mean() * 100)
comp.T.plot(kind='bar', ax=axes[1], color=colors)
axes[1].set_ylabel('% records with data')
axes[1].set_title('Data Completeness per Class')
axes[1].set_xticklabels(axes[1].get_xticklabels(), rotation=35, ha='right')
axes[1].legend(title='Class', fontsize=8)
axes[1].axhline(100, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Block 2 · Structure Standardisation — Canonicalise and Deduplicate¶

When data comes from multiple papers:

  • The same compound may appear under different names or with different SMILES strings
  • Canonicalisation ensures every molecule has exactly one standard SMILES
  • InChIKey comparison detects duplicate structures reliably

Rule: Always standardise SMILES before calculating any descriptors.

In [6]:
# ── 2a: Validate and canonicalise all SMILES ───────────────────

from rdkit.Chem.inchi import MolToInchi, InchiToInchiKey

def standardise(smiles):
    """Return (canonical_smiles, inchikey) or (None, None) if invalid."""
    mol = MolFromSmiles(smiles)
    if mol is None:
        return None, None
    canon = MolToSmiles(mol)
    inchi = MolToInchi(mol)
    key   = InchiToInchiKey(inchi) if inchi else None
    return canon, key

df['CanonSMILES'], df['InChIKey'] = zip(*df['SMILES'].map(standardise))

n_invalid = df['CanonSMILES'].isna().sum()
print(f'Invalid SMILES: {n_invalid}')
print(f'Valid structures: {df["CanonSMILES"].notna().sum()}')

# Show original vs canonical for a few compounds
check = df[['Name','SMILES','CanonSMILES']].head(4).copy()
check['Changed?'] = check['SMILES'] != check['CanonSMILES']

display(check)
"""
display(check.style.hide(axis='index')
        .set_caption('Original vs Canonical SMILES')

Block 4 · Detect and Handle Missing Values¶

Three strategies depending on how many values are missing:

Strategy When to use
Drop rows Target property is missing — cannot use for training
Drop columns >40% of values missing — descriptor is unreliable
Impute (fill) <20% missing — replace with mean/median/mode

Block 5 · Detect and Handle Outliers¶

Outliers can be:

  • Real — a genuinely extreme compound (do not delete without checking)
  • Errors — transcription mistakes from papers (should be corrected)

Detection methods covered:

  1. Box plots (visual)
  2. Z-score (statistical — flags values > 3σ from mean)
  3. IQR fence (robust — flags values beyond 1.5 × IQR)
  4. Isolation Forest (ML-based)
In [16]:
# ── 5a: Box plots — visual outlier detection ──────────────────

df_plot = df_clean[numeric_cols].dropna()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 7))
axes = axes.flatten()

for ax, col in zip(axes, numeric_cols):
    q1, q3 = df_plot[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    iqr    = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr
    outliers = df_clean[['Name', col]].dropna()
    outliers = outliers[(outliers[col] < lo) | (outliers[col] > hi)]

    ax.boxplot(df_plot[col].dropna(), vert=True, patch_artist=True,
               boxprops=dict(facecolor='#AED6F1'))
    # Overlay outlier labels
    for _, row in outliers.iterrows():
        ax.scatter(1, row[col], color='red', zorder=5, s=50)
        ax.annotate(row['Name'], (1, row[col]),
                    textcoords='offset points', xytext=(8, 0), fontsize=7, color='red')
    ax.set_title(col, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xticklabels([])

plt.suptitle('Box Plots — Red dots = IQR-flagged outliers', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# ── 5b: Z-score outlier detection ─────────────────────────────

from scipy import stats as spstats

z_threshold = 2.5   # flag if |z| > 2.5

flagged_rows = []
for col in numeric_cols:
    subset = df_clean[['Name', col]].dropna()
    z      = np.abs(spstats.zscore(subset[col]))
    flagged = subset[z > z_threshold]
    for _, row in flagged.iterrows():
        flagged_rows.append({
            'Compound':  row['Name'],
            'Property':  col,
            'Value':     round(row[col], 2),
            '|Z-score|': round(z[z > z_threshold].iloc[
                list(flagged.index).index(row.name)], 2)
        })

df_flagged = pd.DataFrame(flagged_rows)
if df_flagged.empty:
    print('No outliers flagged at |Z| > 2.5')
else:
    display(df_flagged.sort_values('|Z-score|', ascending=False))
    """
        display(df_flagged.sort_values('|Z-score|', ascending=False)
            .style.hide(axis='index')

Block 6 · Descriptor Calculation and Feature Matrix Assembly¶

Now we calculate molecular descriptors for every compound in the dataset
and assemble the full feature matrix X paired with the target vector y.

We combine:

  • Zero-dimensional descriptors (formula-based)
  • Two-dimensional RDKit descriptors (topology)
  • Morgan fingerprint bits (structural patterns)
In [20]:
# ── 6a: Calculate descriptors for all valid compounds ──────────

fpgen = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=512)

def parse_formula(formula):
    counts = {}
    for elem in ['C','H','N','O']:
        m = re.search(rf'{elem}(\d*)', str(formula))
        counts[elem] = int(m.group(1)) if m and m.group(1) else (1 if m else 0)
    return counts

def calc_all_descriptors(name, smiles, formula, mw):
    """Returns a dict of descriptors for one compound."""
    mol = MolFromSmiles(smiles)
    if mol is None:
        return None

    e  = parse_formula(formula)
    ob = round((1600/mw)*(2*e['C']+e['H']/2-e['O']), 2) if mw else None

    # 0D
    d = {
        'Name':    name,
        'MW':      round(mw, 2),
        'nC':      e['C'], 'nH': e['H'], 'nN': e['N'], 'nO': e['O'],
        'nNO2':    smiles.count('[N+](=O)[O-]'),
        'NC_ratio':round(e['N']/e['C'], 3) if e['C'] else 0,
        'OB_pct':  ob,
    }

    # 2D RDKit
    d.update({
        'TPSA':       round(Descriptors.TPSA(mol), 2),
        'LogP':       round(Descriptors.MolLogP(mol), 3),
        'HBD':        rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumHBD(mol),
        'HBA':        rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumHBA(mol),
        'RotBonds':   rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumRotatableBonds(mol),
        'Rings':      rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumRings(mol),
        'ArRings':    rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumAromaticRings(mol),
        'HeavyAtoms': mol.GetNumHeavyAtoms(),
        'FrCSP3':     round(Descriptors.FractionCSP3(mol), 4),
        'BalabanJ':   round(Descriptors.BalabanJ(mol), 4),
        'Chi0':       round(Descriptors.Chi0(mol), 4),
        'Chi1':       round(Descriptors.Chi1(mol), 4),
        'Kappa1':     round(Descriptors.Kappa1(mol), 4),
    })

    # Morgan fingerprint bits (512-bit)
    fp  = fpgen.GetFingerprint(mol)
    arr = np.zeros(512, dtype=np.uint8)
    DataStructs.ConvertToNumpyArray(fp, arr)
    for i, bit in enumerate(arr):
        d[f'FP{i}'] = int(bit)

    return d

# Calculate for all compounds with valid SMILES
desc_rows = []
for _, row in df_target.iterrows():
    result = calc_all_descriptors(
        row['Name'], row['CanonSMILES'], row['Formula'], row['MW'])
    if result:
        result['ImpactSens_J']  = row['ImpactSens_J']
        result['Density']       = row['Density']
        result['DetVel_ms']     = row['DetVel_ms']
        result['Class']         = row['Class']
        desc_rows.append(result)

df_desc = pd.DataFrame(desc_rows)
print(f'Feature matrix assembled: {df_desc.shape}')
print(f'  {df_desc.shape[0]} compounds  ×  {df_desc.shape[1]} columns')
print(f'  (includes Name, targets, class + {512+13+9} descriptor columns)')

Block 7 · Feature Preprocessing — Filter, Correlation, Scaling¶

Raw descriptor matrices contain:

  • Constant or near-constant columns (useless — remove)
  • Highly correlated pairs (redundant — remove one)
  • Different scales (unfair advantage — normalise)

This block walks through each step.

In [22]:

vt = VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01)   # remove columns with variance < 0.01
X_vt = vt.fit_transform(X_raw)

removed_var = X_raw.shape[1] - X_vt.shape[1]
kept_cols   = X_raw.columns[vt.get_support()].tolist()

print(f'Before variance filter: {X_raw.shape[1]} features')

In [24]:
# ── 7c: Step 2 — remove highly correlated descriptor pairs ─────

def remove_high_corr(df_feat, threshold=0.90):
    """Remove one feature from each pair with |correlation| > threshold."""
    corr_mat = df_feat.corr().abs()
    upper    = corr_mat.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr_mat.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
    to_drop  = [col for col in upper.columns if any(upper[col] > threshold)]
    return df_feat.drop(columns=to_drop), to_drop

X_uncorr, dropped_corr = remove_high_corr(X_df, threshold=0.90)

print(f'After variance filter:    {X_df.shape[1]} features')
print(f'Removed (corr > 0.90):    {len(dropped_corr)}')

Block 8 · Train / Test Splitting — Random and Scaffold-Based¶

The golden rule: never evaluate a model on data it was trained on.

Two splitting strategies:

Method When to use Pros / Cons
Random split Quick baseline Fast; similar molecules may end up in both sets
Scaffold split Realistic evaluation Similar molecules stay together; harder test

# ── 8b: Scaffold-based split (keeps similar structures together) 

def get_scaffold(smiles):
    """Return Murcko scaffold SMILES, or empty string for acyclics."""
    mol = MolFromSmiles(smiles)
    if mol is None:
        return ''
    try:
        scaffold = MurckoScaffold.GetScaffoldForMol(mol)
        return MolToSmiles(scaffold)
    except Exception:
        return ''

# Assign scaffold to each compound
df_scaffold = df_raw[['Name','SMILES']].copy()
df_scaffold.columns = ['Name','SMILES']
df_scaffold['Scaffold'] = df_scaffold['SMILES'].map(get_scaffold)

Block 9 · Full Pipeline — SMILES to ML-Ready Matrix¶

This block assembles everything from Blocks 0–8 into one clean, reusable function.
Give it a list of (name, SMILES, target_value) tuples and it returns train/test arrays ready for scikit-learn.

This is what you would use as your starting point for any new dataset.

In [31]:
# ── 9a: Complete pipeline function ────────────────────────────

def build_em_dataset(records, target_key='ImpactSens_J',
                     fp_bits=512, corr_threshold=0.90,
                     var_threshold=0.01, test_size=0.30,
                     random_state=42, scale='standard'):
    """
    records : list of dicts with keys Name, SMILES, Formula, MW, <target_key>, ...
    Returns : X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, feature_names, scaler
    """
    fpgen = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=fp_bits)

    # ── Step 1: validate and canonicalise ──────────────────────
    valid = []
    for rec in records:
        mol = MolFromSmiles(rec['SMILES'])
        if mol is None or rec.get(target_key) is None:
            continue
        rec['CanonSMILES'] = MolToSmiles(mol)
        rec['mol']         = mol
        valid.append(rec)
    print(f'[1] Valid records with target: {len(valid)}')

    # ── Step 2: deduplicate by InChIKey ────────────────────────
    seen, deduped = set(), []
    for rec in valid:
        inchi = MolToInchi(rec['mol'])
        key   = InchiToInchiKey(inchi) if inchi else rec['CanonSMILES']
        if key not in seen:
            seen.add(key)
            deduped.append(rec)
    print(f'[2] After deduplication:        {len(deduped)}')

    # ── Step 3: calculate descriptors ─────────────────────────
    rows, targets, names_out = [], [], []
    for rec in deduped:
        mol = rec['mol']
        e   = parse_formula(rec.get('Formula',''))
        mw  = float(rec.get('MW', Descriptors.MolWt(mol)))
        ob  = round((1600/mw)*(2*e['C']+e['H']/2-e['O']), 2)

        d = {
            'nNO2':   rec['CanonSMILES'].count('[N+](=O)[O-]'),
            'nN':     e['N'], 'nO': e['O'], 'nC': e['C'],
            'MW':     mw, 'OB_pct': ob,
            'TPSA':   Descriptors.TPSA(mol),
            'LogP':   Descriptors.MolLogP(mol),
            'HBD':    rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumHBD(mol),
            'HBA':    rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumHBA(mol),
            'Rings':  rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumRings(mol),
            'FrCSP3': Descriptors.FractionCSP3(mol),
            'Chi0':   Descriptors.Chi0(mol),
            'Kappa1': Descriptors.Kappa1(mol),
        }
        fp  = fpgen.GetFingerprint(mol)
        arr = np.zeros(fp_bits, dtype=np.uint8)
        DataStructs.ConvertToNumpyArray(fp, arr)
        for i, bit in enumerate(arr):
            d[f'FP{i}'] = int(bit)

        rows.append(d)
        targets.append(float(rec[target_key]))
        names_out.append(rec['Name'])

    X_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    y_arr = np.array(targets)
    print(f'[3] Descriptor matrix:          {X_df.shape}')

    # ── Step 4: variance filter ────────────────────────────────
    vt = VarianceThreshold(threshold=var_threshold)
    X_vt = vt.fit_transform(X_df)
    feat_names = X_df.columns[vt.get_support()].tolist()
    print(f'[4] After variance filter:      {len(feat_names)} features')

    # ── Step 5: correlation filter ─────────────────────────────
    X_tmp  = pd.DataFrame(X_vt, columns=feat_names)
    X_unc, dropped = remove_high_corr(X_tmp, corr_threshold)
    print(f'[5] After correlation filter:   {X_unc.shape[1]} features')

    # ── Step 6: scale ──────────────────────────────────────────
    scaler = StandardScaler() if scale == 'standard' else MinMaxScaler()
    X_sc   = scaler.fit_transform(X_unc)

    # ── Step 7: train/test split ───────────────────────────────
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te, n_tr, n_te = train_test_split(
        X_sc, y_arr, names_out,
        test_size=test_size, random_state=random_state
    )
    print(f'[6] Train: {len(X_tr)}, Test: {len(X_te)}')
    print(f'    Train compounds: {list(n_tr)}')
    print(f'    Test  compounds: {list(n_te)}')

    return X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te, X_unc.columns.tolist(), scaler

print('Pipeline function defined. Run Block 9b to execute it.')

Pipeline function defined. Run Block 9b to execute it.

# ── 9c: Quick sanity check — train a simple model ─────────────
# (Full modelling is covered in Chapter 4)

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics  import r2_score, mean_absolute_error

rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_train = rf.predict(X_train)
y_pred_test  = rf.predict(X_test)

r2_train = r2_score(y_train, y_pred_train)
r2_test  = r2_score(y_test,  y_pred_test)
mae_test = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_test)

print(f'Sanity check — Random Forest on cleaned dataset:')
print(f'  R² training : {r2_train:.3f}')
print(f'  R² test     : {r2_test:.3f}')
print(f'  MAE test    : {mae_test:.2f} J')
print()
print('Training R² >> Test R² means some overfitting — expected with n=20.')
print('Larger datasets and cross-validation address this (see Chapter 4).')

# Observed vs predicted plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.5))
ax.scatter(y_train, y_pred_train, color='steelblue', alpha=0.8,
           label=f'Train R²={r2_train:.2f}', s=60)
ax.scatter(y_test, y_pred_test, color='tomato', alpha=0.9,
           label=f'Test  R²={r2_test:.2f}',  s=80, marker='D')

lims = [0, df_desc['ImpactSens_J'].max()*1.1]
ax.plot(lims, lims, 'k--', linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel('Observed Impact Sensitivity (J)')
ax.set_ylabel('Predicted Impact Sensitivity (J)')
ax.set_title('Observed vs Predicted — Sanity Check')
ax.legend()
ax.set_xlim(lims); ax.set_ylim(lims)

Summary — What You Learned in Chapter 3¶

Block Concept Key Python tool
0 Build a 30-compound literature dataset pandas.DataFrame
1 Data quality audit — missing values, stats, class balance pd.isna, describe, matplotlib
2 Canonicalise SMILES, detect duplicates via InChIKey MolToSmiles, InchiToInchiKey
3 Visualise distributions, pairplots, correlations seaborn.pairplot, heatmap
4 Handle missing values — drop, mean, KNN imputation SimpleImputer, KNNImputer
5 Detect outliers — boxplot, Z-score, Isolation Forest scipy.stats.zscore, IsolationForest
6 Calculate descriptors + fingerprints, assemble X matrix Descriptors, rdFingerprintGenerator
7 Remove low-variance & correlated features; scale X VarianceThreshold, StandardScaler
8 Random and scaffold-based train/test splits train_test_split, MurckoScaffold
9 End-to-end pipeline: SMILES → ML-ready arrays All of the above combined
